scaling.heading: Scaling an API
scaling.question: How would you scale an API to handle 1 million requests per second?
scaling.intro: No single trick gets you there. Turn on one layer at a time and see which bottleneck it removes, and what it costs.

core.label: API server
core.detail: A single server is the first bottleneck: one machine's CPU, memory and connections.

components.label: API architecture
components.solves: Keeps each request cheap: stateless handlers, pagination, rate limiting and idempotent endpoints so servers can be added and requests can be retried safely.
components.tradeoff: Statelessness pushes session and state into shared stores.

components.label: Load balancing
components.solves: Spreads incoming traffic across servers and removes the single point of failure at the entrance.
components.tradeoff: The balancer itself must be redundant, and health checks must be accurate.

components.label: Horizontal scaling
components.solves: Adds more identical API servers instead of a bigger one, so capacity grows with traffic.
components.tradeoff: Shared resources such as the database become the next bottleneck.

components.label: Caching
components.solves: Answers repeated reads from memory so most requests never reach the database.
components.tradeoff: Stale data and cache invalidation are hard problems.

components.label: Databases
components.solves: Read replicas absorb read traffic, and partitioning (sharding) splits writes across machines.
components.tradeoff: Replication lag and cross-partition queries add complexity.

components.label: Kafka
components.solves: Moves slow or bursty work off the request path onto an event stream, so the API responds quickly and workers process at their own pace.
components.tradeoff: Work becomes asynchronous: ordering, retries and eventual consistency need design.
